# Shadow Futures: Full Context for Language Models

Canonical website: https://shadow-futures.vercel.app/
Paper landing page: https://shadow-futures.vercel.app/paper
PDF: https://shadow-futures.vercel.app/paper.pdf
Author: Martin Erlic
First posted: December 2025
Revised: July 2026
DOI: 10.2139/ssrn.6003994
SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6003994

## Canonical title

Shadow Futures: Contribution Uncertainty and the Self-Reinforcing Market

## Abstract

Can a market observe productive inputs perfectly and still be unable to learn what those inputs contributed to its rewards? This paper studies adaptive allocation systems in which verified work, effort, measurable quality, cost, foregone income, and capital at risk directly affect reward probabilities, while past reward changes future exposure. I define the market's comparison budget as the cumulative probability mass remaining outside the currently dominant alternative. For a broad class of locally equivalent allocation rules with a common predictable design, finite total comparison makes the complete single-history laws generated by distinct contribution parameters mutually absolutely continuous. No estimator based on one realized market can consistently recover every nonconstant contribution functional, and no test can separate two contribution parameters with vanishing total error. A finite-horizon bound shows that attribution precision is limited by the comparison budget rather than transaction count. Strong reinforcement is a sharp corollary because it exhausts the budget and produces eventual allocation monopoly. With latent position, contribution and position can be exactly observationally equivalent. The unrealized paths needed to separate these explanations are shadow futures. The result does not deny that work or risk matters. It shows that a real causal effect can remain unrecoverable from the path that rewarded it, with implications for platforms, competition policy, entrepreneurship, and merit-sensitive taxation.

## Short explanation

Increasing returns and preferential attachment explain why an early lead can compound. Shadow Futures asks a different question: after a market has reinforced one path, can the observed record tell us how much productive inputs caused the resulting rewards?

The answer can be no even when productive inputs are perfectly observed and directly affect every reward probability. Once a dominant alternative receives nearly all later opportunities, later transactions mostly repeat the existing lead. They do not create an unlimited supply of independent comparisons.

Transaction count is therefore not the same as comparison. A market can be extremely active while producing very little new evidence about what would have happened under plausible alternative allocations.

## Core definitions

Shadow futures are unrealized positive-probability market histories with the same productive inputs, rules, and initial state but different allocation shocks and terminal rewards.

Contribution uncertainty is uncertainty about how much observed productive inputs causally contributed to realized rewards after those inputs passed through a self-reinforcing allocation process.

The comparison budget is the cumulative probability mass remaining outside the currently dominant alternative. It measures how much genuine competitive comparison the market can still produce.

Epistemic monopoly is control over the production of the independent comparison paths needed to explain an allocation. It concerns control over evidence, not only control over output or price.

## Model

For agent i at time t:

s_i,t(beta) = exp(beta x_i) (a + N_i(t))^rho

p_i,t(beta) = s_i,t(beta) / sum_j s_j,t(beta)

epsilon_t(beta) = 1 - max_i p_i,t(beta)

B_T(beta) = sum from t = 0 to T - 1 of epsilon_t(beta)

x_i is a verified contribution-related input. beta measures how strongly that input affects the next allocation. N_i(t) is accumulated attention, customers, sales, or another market-specific stock. rho is reinforcement strength. p_i,t is the conditional probability of the next allocation. epsilon_t is the probability that the next allocation goes to someone other than the current favorite. B_T is cumulative comparison through time T.

## Central theorem

Under a common predictable design, local equivalence of one-step laws, two-sided Hellinger control by remaining comparison, and finite total comparison under the parameters being compared:

B_infinity(beta) < infinity for every beta being compared
implies
P_beta and P_beta-prime are mutually absolutely continuous
implies
no estimator based on one complete realized history can consistently recover every nonconstant contribution functional F(beta).

The complete-history laws are not claimed to be equal. Mutual absolute continuity means they overlap too much for one realized market history to support universal consistent recovery of the contribution parameter. The same logic prevents tests from separating two contribution parameters with vanishing total error.

## Finite-horizon implication

Attribution precision is limited by cumulative comparison rather than raw transaction count. When the comparison budget grows slowly, a long record can still contain limited information about contribution.

## Strong reinforcement

Strong reinforcement is a sharp corollary, not the definition of the theorem. In the paper's finite-agent reinforced allocation model, sufficiently strong reinforcement exhausts the comparison budget and produces eventual allocation monopoly. One alternative eventually receives all but finitely many rewards.

## Latent position

If market position is not fully observed, contribution and position can be exactly observationally equivalent. A change in the contribution coefficient can be offset by a change in latent position, leaving every conditional allocation probability and every observable history law unchanged.

## What the result does and does not say

The result does not say that work, effort, quality, cost, foregone income, capital, or risk have no causal effect. Those variables can genuinely change reward probabilities.

The result says that a real causal effect may remain unrecoverable from the one path that rewarded it. Real contribution is not the same as identifiable contribution.

The result is not merely a claim about inequality, power laws, preferential attachment, or increasing returns. Those concepts describe concentration or the mechanism of cumulative advantage. Shadow Futures identifies a limit on what the resulting record can teach us about contribution.

A Lorenz curve or final market share describes the distribution of rewards. It does not, by itself, identify how much of that distribution was caused by contribution, position, reinforcement, or realized allocation shocks.

The website simulation illustrates the mechanism. It is not empirical proof of the theorem and is not a forecast for a particular platform or industry.

## Applications

- Creator platforms and recommendation systems
- Competitive firms, entrepreneurship, and platform markets
- AI labs, chips, cloud computing, and data centers
- AI agents, machine-to-machine payments, and the agentic economy
- Technical standards, procurement, finance, and distribution
- Antitrust, merger review, interoperability, and independent experimentation
- Progressive taxation, universal basic income, and social dividends

## Design implications

Learning can be preserved by creating genuinely independent comparisons. Examples include meaningful randomized exposure for newcomers, independent starts or resets, portability, multihoming, open standards, structural separation, independent procurement, and public options.

Random exposure is an intervention because it changes the allocation rule. It is not merely passive measurement of the original reinforced market.

## Policy boundary

The theorem does not calculate an individual's exact luck, rent, or deserved share. It shows why extreme market rewards are not precise certificates of individual contribution when the market has consumed the comparisons needed for attribution.

Tax rates, public ownership, universal basic income, social dividends, and other distributive institutions remain collective choices. The research supports making those choices openly around power, security, freedom, and shared prosperity rather than treating a reinforced market ranking as a neutral measurement of merit.
